part_a_stack_depth_guard.risk: ElectricalTimingTree.cc:131-136's own TODO warns of stack overflow on recursive crit-path extraction 'with long chains of logic (4000+ nodes)'.
part_a_stack_depth_guard.method: extractCritPathDelay() instrumented with a global current-depth counter (incremented on entry, decremented on every return path, tracking the max seen) and a total-nodes-visited counter. Measured via performCritPathExtract(getNet("CK")) on a standalone DFFRAM at the 4 canonical points, and on a full Router (P=5 in/out ports, V=4 VCs, 1 VN, 32-entry buffers/VC, 64-bit flits, DFFRAM buffer model, BroadcastHTree router-level clock tree per configs/router.cfg's own convention) from its own "CK" net.
part_a_stack_depth_guard.interpretation: Recursion DEPTH (what actually consumes C++ call-stack frames in a depth-first walk -- siblings pop off the stack before the next sibling is explored, so stack usage tracks the longest single root-to-leaf path, not total graph size) stays in the tens to low hundreds across every configuration measured, including the largest DFFRAM point and a full multi-VC Router. Total NODES VISITED grows into the hundreds of thousands at large N (driven by the N-way row fanout each getting its own DFS sub-call), but that drives wall-clock time, not stack depth -- it is a separate quantity from the TODO's actual stack-overflow concern.
part_a_stack_depth_guard.margin_against_4000: Worst measured depth is 164 (Router, P=5/V=4) -> margin = 4000/164 = 24.4x. Worst DFFRAM-only point is 81 (512,256) -> margin = 49.4x. Both comfortably above the 2x threshold.
part_a_stack_depth_guard.reasoning: The TODO's own '4000+ nodes' framing describes a hypothetical single long SERIAL chain (where depth == node count); DSENT's actual graphs (DFFRAM, Router) are branching/fanning structures where depth stays governed by the longest single gate-to-gate chain (roughly: CKGate0 -> INV_CKGate0 -> EnBuf stages -> CKGate1 -> INV_CKGate1 -> RowBuf stages -> DFF.CK -> internal CK-to-Q -> Mux tree -> Out, on the order of 50-160 hops even at the largest configurations tested), not by total fanout breadth. No rewrite triggered per the task's own '>=2x margin -> leave as-is' instruction.

part_b_local_interconnect_underestimate.readme_reference: README:357-359 (bug #4): "Local interconnect will have an ever-larger impact on power and timing as technology scales... we have not implemented a method for automatically estimating them... Evaluations for 22nm [and below should be treated with this in mind]" -- this project's own tech file is tech/tech_models/Bulk22LVT.model, i.e. exactly the node this bug flags.
part_b_local_interconnect_underestimate.what_is_modelled: CellMacros.cc:322-327 (updateInverter, and the equivalent block in every other cell macro) adds an INTRA-CELL metal-1 stub: wire_length = folds * cell_height, wire_cap = calculateWireCapacitance("Metal1", ...). This estimates the wiring INSIDE one standard cell (from the transistor drain to the cell's own output pin, scaled by how many parallel fingers ('folds') the cell's drive strength requires) and is baked into that cell's cached, load-independent self-capacitance (Part 1.3 of the earlier investigation report). It is NOT inter-cell routing.
part_b_local_interconnect_underestimate.what_is_not_modelled: Every net DFFRAM.cc creates via createNet() is a bare ElectricalNet with m_distributed_cap_=m_distributed_res_=0 (the ElectricalNet constructor default) -- DFFRAM.cc never calls setDistributedCap()/setDistributedRes() on any of its own nets (only BroadcastHTree.cc/RepeatedLink.cc do that, for their own internal wire-model levels, and DFFRAM no longer uses either of those after Phase 4.1). So the wire connecting one gate's output to the next gate's input carries exactly zero capacitance and zero resistance, everywhere in DFFRAM.
zero_wire_load_nets_read_path: DFF_Out<i> (each row's Q output, feeding the Mux, per entry)

quantification.method: DSENT's own calculateWireCapacitance(), Local metal layer (tech/tech_models/Bulk22LVT.model: 32nm min width/spacing, same formula the codebase already applies to BroadcastHTree/RepeatedLink, just not applied inside DFFRAM), evaluated via the wire_diag temporary subcommand.
quantification.reference_gate_load: Minimum-size (X1) NAND2/INV/BUF A_Cap = 4.52571e-16 F (from the StdCellLib cache, same for all three -- input cap is set by transistor gate width, roughly independent of gate function).

row_enable_fanout_special_case.reason: Unlike every other net in the list above, the net feeding all N NAND2_CKGate1_i A pins (the row-enable chain's own output) is not a short point-to-point hop -- it must physically span the DFFRAM array, whose footprint the codebase itself already computes as SitePitch=sqrt(array_area) (this is exactly the quantity the OLD BroadcastHTree/EnableTree was sized against before Phase 4.1, and Router.cc's own top-level ClockTree still is).
row_enable_fanout_special_case.caveat: A real layout would route a span this large on Intermediate/Global metal, not Local (Local's own per-length resistance/capacitance is not representative at hundreds of um) -- this number is an upper-bound sanity check using the SAME layer/formula already used elsewhere in the codebase, not a claim that this is the physically correct value on the correct layer.

part_b_local_interconnect_underestimate.conclusion: The missing interconnect capacitance is NOT uniform across DFFRAM. For genuinely local, point-to-point hops (RowBuf chain stages, INV_CKGate1_i->DFF.CK, and by extension the read path's Dec_Out/DFF_Out/Mux_Out nets, all cell-adjacent in a real layout) the missing term is small, plausibly a few percent to ~20% of one gate's input capacitance for a 1-4 gate-pitch hop -- consistent with README bug #4's framing as a real but second-order effect at this node. For the ROW-ENABLE FANOUT net specifically, which must span the array's full physical extent, the missing term is potentially the DOMINANT capacitance at large N/B (>100x a single gate's input cap at (512,256), by this same-formula estimate) -- and this is a direct, disclosed side effect of the EnBuf-chain fix (Closure predecessor task): replacing BroadcastHTree correctly fixed a topology mismatch (Part 2.2 of the earlier investigation, NumberLevels tied to log2(N) rather than real electrical fanout) but also removed the ONLY wire term that specific net had. No wire model added here, per instructions -- reported as a disclosed limitation and written into scripts/run_buffer_sweep.py's ASSUMPTIONS list (item 8) so every sweep run carries this caveat in its own meta.assumptions field.

part_d_iso_capacity_headline.distributions: 128 buffers x 4 entries, 16 buffers x 32 entries, 1 buffer x 512 entries -- all B=128, 65536 total bits, frequency=1e9 Hz, timing_opt=false
part_d_iso_capacity_headline.methodology: Standalone DFFRAM per distribution point (via the temporary dffram_diag harness / buffer_characteristics with matching (N,B)). AREA and LEAKAGE are the per-buffer value multiplied by buffer_count (every buffer instance exists in silicon simultaneously, all the time). e_read, e_write, and t_critical are the PER-BUFFER value only, not summed across the distribution -- a single read or write access touches exactly one buffer in a many-small-buffers system, and a critical path is inherently a per-instance property, never additive. This is the interpretation that reproduces the task-stated baseline's order of magnitude (see below); the alternative 'N VCs sharing one physical RAM' interpretation, tried in a prior session (docs/phase6_final_validation_results.json, part_d), produced e_read/t_critical ratios of ~1.1x/1.0x -- two orders of magnitude off the stated reference -- and is not reused here.
part_d_iso_capacity_headline.reproduction_note: The 'before' (H-tree era) numbers measured here -- area_spread=1.65%, e_read_ratio=134.8x, t_critical_ratio=7.44x -- are the right order of magnitude and correct qualitative shape against the task-stated reference (0.9% / 121.5x / 8.9x), but not an exact match, most likely because this measurement's exact software revision (P5 activity params + VC-select fix already applied to RouterInputPort.cc, frequency=1e9, timing_opt=false) differs from whatever produced the original stated numbers. This is disclosed rather than forced to match.

headline_answer_per_metric.area: UNCHANGED (gap neither narrowed nor widened materially): 1.646% -> 1.661% spread, a +0.9%-relative widening that is well within measurement/rounding noise for a fix that only touches DFFRAM's own row-enable structure, not the DFF array or decoder that dominate area.
headline_answer_per_metric.leakage: UNCHANGED: 1.345% -> 1.320% spread, a negligible narrowing, same reasoning as area.
headline_answer_per_metric.e_read: EXACTLY UNCHANGED: 134.8204x both before and after, to the digit shown -- confirms (yet again, now at the whole-distribution level) that this fix never touches the read path.
headline_answer_per_metric.e_write: NEGLIGIBLY NARROWED: 87.546x -> 87.206x, a ~0.4% relative narrowing -- present but small, consistent with the P4->P4' e_write deltas (mean -2.99%) being of similar small magnitude at every individual point and therefore nearly cancelling in a max/min ratio.
headline_answer_per_metric.t_critical: SUBSTANTIALLY NARROWED -- the headline result: 7.439x -> 3.891x, very nearly HALVED (-47.7% relative reduction in the ratio). This is because the fix's t_critical improvement is far larger in absolute terms for the LARGE, single-buffer end of the range (the 1x512 point improves from 7.649e-10s to 3.489e-10s, a 54.4% cut) than for the many-small-buffers end (the 128x4 point improves from 1.028e-10s to 8.968e-11s, a 12.8% cut) -- exactly what Part C's own P4->P4' ledger row already showed as a general pattern (t_critical improvement magnitude grows with N).

part_d_iso_capacity_headline.conclusion: For the original research question this project was built around -- comparing many-small-buffers against few-large-buffers switch architectures at equal total capacity -- this closure task's fix materially changes the answer along exactly one axis: the two architectures' CRITICAL-PATH/frequency-capability gap is now much smaller (nearly half) than it was under the old BroadcastHTree-based clock distribution, while the area/leakage/energy story is essentially unchanged. A comparison that leaned on the old timing gap to argue for one architecture over the other would need to be revisited; a comparison based on area or energy would not.
